Hon. J. A. ROBB (Acting Minister of Finance) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide that goods produced or manufactured in Finland shall receive treatment as favourable as that accorded to goods produced or manufactured in any foreign country so long as goods produced or manufactured in Canada enjoy in Finland the same treatment as is enjoyed by similar goods produced or manufactured in the United Kingdom, as set out in Article 23 of the Treaty of Commerce and Navigation between the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and Finland, made at Helsingfors the 14th day of December, 1923.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

The House will readily
see the great difference between this resolution as a matter of both form and substance and the resolution which we were asked to pass as the antecedent to the Grain Act. This resolution at least sets out what nature of legislation the government intends. Would the minister be good enough to give us a review of the history of the enactment?-that is to say: what has led up to this; what has been our trade relations with England; how has it come about that we have entered into this arrangement; and specifically what is Canada to get in return for the concessions made.

This will involve practically
the same legislation as we had last year in a bill that was passed through this House without very much objection if any, but that was defeated in the Upper Chamber. As my right hon. friend knows, the population of Fin-203i
land is about 3,335,000. The trade of Canada with Finland has been considerable and it is a favourable trade for Canada. For instance, for the ten months ended January, 1925, the total importations from Finland amounted to $13,581 and the total exportations to Finland of goods produced in Canada amounted to $908,777. The imports from Finland include the following:
Cream separators	 $2,187
Wrapping paper, kraft	 2,777
Tissue paper	 3,842
Other paper and	manufactures of.. ..	628
The total of that would be only a few thousand.

Yes, just a few thousand on kraft paper. When this goes through they will come under the French treaty which is 201 per cent on this particular article, and the present tariff being 25 per cent they will then have an advantage of 4| per cent. The total imports into Finland of kraft paper amounted to $2,777. Our exports to Finland are largely of farm products. The list is as follows:
Flour	 $787,995
Oatmeal and rolled	oats	 50,751
Clover seed	 2,880
Lard	 4,984
Felt	 6,060
Pipe and tubing	 11,695
Adding and calculating	machines	 18,000
Woodworking machinery	 4,095
Automobiles	 17,058
All other items	 5,259
Total	 $908,777
What is the duty on flour entering Finland?
Finland has two tariffs, a general and a conventional. I have no record of the duty on flour, but the duty on passenger automobiles under the general tariff is 20 per cent.
Is there any duty on flour into Finland? I should not think so.

There is a duty on flour and I will tell my hon. friend why I think so. The matter was brought to my attention last year by one who I think is the largest miller in Canada. He was complaining that this trade agreement had been killed in the Senate and those to whom he made the complaint retorted that this had been done by his own friends, the kraft people; for it so happened that he was also president of a kraft mill. He was disturbed because it meant a loss of trade in some way to him. The duty on passenger automobiles is 20 per cent under the general tariff and per cent under the conventional tariff, and that I
Canada-Finland Treaty

think is a fair indication of the general trend of the duties. Under article 5 of the treaty we shall be entitled to whatever favoured nation concessions Finland gives. There is no preference in regard to flour but there is a duty of about 2 cents per kilogram.

Are the imports from
Finland limited to those coming direct through Canadian ports, as is the case in other treaties?

Yes; the imports under all
favoured nation concessions come through Canadian ports.
I do not think the minister fancies that he has given us even a fraction of the information we ought to have before coming to a conclusion.
If my right hon. friend desires more I shall be glad to give it.

Here we are proposing
to give concessions to Finland in respect of a very important article of Canadian produce, an article in respect of which Finland is in the world to-day a very keen competitor. It may be wise to give these concessions if we get sufficient to return, but I fancy that no hon. member has yet received from the minister information in regard to one single thing we get in return. He says that we shall get the conventional tariff subject to certain conditions. That compels us to look at our exports and see whether .these concessions are any good to us. Our principal export to Finland is flour; I gather from the minister's figures that it is more than al'l the rest together, four times over. And the minister tells us that he does net know whether or not there is a duty on this commodity into Finland.

I said there was a duty but
no preference.

But we need to know
not only that there is a duty but what it is, whether or not it is to be changed by the treaty, and if so to what extent. That is the principal single item of our exports to that country, over-shadowing all the others, and we ought to know something about it.

I have told the committee
already that there is a small duty on flour but no preference. But I submit that there is a considerable advantage to Canada in having this treaty go through. I know where the opposition to this treaty comes from; It was the subject of a boast in the upper house last year. It was then stated that the opposition came from the kraft people. But

surely Canada need not be afraid of this treaty so far as our kraft imports are concerned, the total from Finland! being, as I have said, some $2,777. We are getting concessions on automobiles and other products and with these, in a market of 3,500,000 people, we shall be able to develop some business. What is the situation in regard to the kraft mills of Canada? The production in Canada was $4,000,000 and there was imported $5,464,000 of wrapping. The production of manilla paper was $4,464,198 and! all other wrapping paper $3,201,976, or a total production of $7,666,174. There was imported into Canada from all countries during the fiscal year ending March 31, 1924, $564,890, making a total for production and imports of $8,231,064. That was the production and importations.
Production of what?

Of kraft and wrapping papers
in Canada. What were the exports? Let us keep in mind1 that the total quantity that came in from Finland was $2,770, but during that period Canada exported $3,153,515. And they are afraid of an importation, of less than $3,000!
What is the duty on kraft?

I gave that a few moments
ago-25 per cent. Under this agreement Finland will get a duty of 20i per cent; she will have a preference of 4| per cent. My hon. friend referred to the question of flour. We have representations made to us on behalf of the Canadian Millers' Association, and I quote a letter addressed to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, (Mr. Low) on March 7, 1924:
I understand negotiations are pending with regard to a commercial treaty between the United States and Finland.
The United States are our competitors in exporting flour.
I believe that a commercial treaty now exists between Great Britain and Finland and I believe Canadian goods would come within this treaty.
As the Finnish trade in flour is still in the hands of United States mills to a large extent, we would like to suggest that some action be taken through your department to protect the interests of Canadian flour shippers in the event of this treaty between the United States and Finland working to our detriment.
This is a valuable market and one we would like to maintain.
For the moment I had quite forgotten that the United States were negotiating for a special treaty with Finland.
Who signs that letter?

F. C. Cornell, who at that
time was secretary of the Canadian Millers' Association.

Canada-Finland Treaty

I 'do not think we have
mluch light yet. We are clear on one thing only-at least I am; we are conceding to Finland a reduction of duty on kraft paper from 25 to 20i per cent. The minister starts out by saying that he knows where the opposition is coming from. I have not seen any yet. I am endeavouring to get some light. If the minister wants to throw an aspersion on any member of this House,-
No.

-that he has been influenced by any kraft paper man or anybody else not to do what is in the public interest, I hurl it back. I tell him first, that neither last session nor this did any kraft paper man speak to me directly, indirectly or in any other way with respect to the Finnish treaty of last session or this, nor did I know until now that this was a re-introduction of the Finnish treaty in another form. I assume the makers of kraft paper would be opposed to any tariff concessions. That is not something to introduce into the debate as a sort of sinister feature likely to colour the actions of hon. members. I set out to find what we are giving and what we are getting. We have learned a lot of what we are giving-4J per cent on kraft paper. I am not yet informed what we are giving in respect of other papers, or if we are giving anything.
We are giving them our intermediate column on all business.

It is considerable, but just what it means one does not know. One has to analyse the business to ascertain whether it is important or not. When we come to the other side we have very little, so far as specific application is concerned, to enlighten us on what we are giving, except as to kraft paper. We do not know what its application is specifically. Going the other way, we find our exports of flour are $500,000.
They are $700,000.
That is still more. The next highest is $50,000, and the rest is very, very small, $6,000. So flour overshadows all other exports many, many times over.
It does.

The minister tells us immediately afterwards what we get. There is a duty on flour into Finland, there is -no preference to anybody. So we are not getting anything on flour, and what the letter of Mr. Cornell had to do with flour I do not know.
Naturally he was anxious that, if necessary, steps should be taken to prevent the United States getting anything better than we are getting.
That is it.

But, first of all, we do
not know if the United States has got anything, and, in the second place, according to this resolution we would not be protecting ourselves at all. This resolution merely says that Finland shall give in respect of our goods as low a tariff as she gives the United Kingdom -not as low as she gives the United States.

She gives the United Kingdom the most favoured nation treatment, and if she gives the United States anything lower than is now contained in the arrangement with the United Kingdom, automatically the United Kingdom will receive the same treatment.

She does not give the
most favoured nation treatment to anybody on flour. Of course, in the future she might. That letter was written a year ago last March, and the United States cannot possibly have any preference on flour, because the minister has already said there is no preference to any nation on flour.
Not yet.

And I would not presume that the negotiations are continuing. As a matter of fact the United States do not make treaties with any other nation giving a preference in their markets. I think the minister will have to admit that the United States make their tariff as they think best suits themselves, and they give no preferential treatment to any country except to Cuba, which is part of themselves. So there is not any bugaboo to be afraid of there. In respect of flour, then, we get absolutely nothing. The minister suggested that we get something on automobiles-he did not tell us what it was. I should like to know what it is. But I do not want any hon. members to be under the delusion that we are getting something in respect of our great flour export business to Finland, for we are getting nothing at all.
* We are getting a concession on automobile wheels. The duty is 20 per cent under the general tariff, and we will get per cent.

Do we sell them any
automobile wheels?
Canada-Finland Treaty
We have a pile of correspondence from the manufacturers of automobiles and agricultural implements urging us to get this concession put through.
I think it would be not at all unlikely that we would be selling them automobile wheels, but I should like to know for sure.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if it does not strike hon. members as rather curious, or at all events as rather signficant. that this and all similar questions are usually discussed wholly from the standpoint of our interests as producers. I hear constantly about "giving" and "getting." Now, I submitted to the House the other day, that public policy, particularly in such matters, ought to be based on the interests of the citizens as consumers rather than as producers. And yet day after day, week after week, year after year, public policy is debated here and elsewhere wholly, or almost wholly, from the standpoint of our interests as producers. My right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) talks about our "giving " concessions to Finnish producers: they are " getting " something if we " give " them a market; we are " getting " something if they "give " us a market. If we give to Finnish producers a market here, are we not entitled to consider what we are getting as buyers? I submit that we are looking at these questions in a topsy-turvy way. I am astonished, disturbed and discouraged at the persistent upside down attitude of the people toward these matters. There is sound ground for the view that public policy ought to be based on our interests as consumers rather than on our interests as producers. I submitted argument in that connection the other night when speaking on the budget. But apparently nobody ever dreams in these discussions of considering the interests of Canadian citizens as consumers. Personally I am in favour of freer trade relations with any country and I think this measure is perfectly in order whether we are getting or giving, because if we can break down these trade harriers producers and consumers are both bound to benefit. I rose only to call the attention of the committee to the very curious situation that faces us.

Replying to my right hon.
friend (Mr. Meighen), the general tariff on passenger motor cars is 20 per cent. We will get the conventional tariff, 8f per cent.
Have we sent them any?
Yes, in the fiscal year ending in 1924 we sent them $13,523 worth.
About six cars.

I quoted the tariff a moment ago, but I might mention that there is a duty per kilo on passenger motor cars not weighing more than 900 kilogrammes. The general tariff is 3.50 markkas, the conventional tariff is 1.81 markkas. For those over 900 kilogrammes the genera! tariff is 5 markkas and the conventional tariff 2.18 markkas.

If we are selling even
six cars to Finland it is something, but it is rather picayune as yet, I am afraid. I am always grateful to be set right and be put back on my feet instead of my head by the hon. member for Brant. I entirely agree that we are all consumers in this world, and in Canada we are not only consumers, but under the present policy we are being consumed. I think I got the right application of the hon. member's theory; that the lower our duties are the better for us, because it will be easier to live. On the same principle the higher Finland has hers the better for us, because if we cannot sell them our wheat it will make wheat cheaper here. No doubt the hon. member is very anxious, therefore, to get wheat down so that people can live more cheaply in Canada. People always talk on these points until they get responsibility, then they begin to think more seriously. In this case it is just a matter of whether or not a trade arrangement adds to the productive industry of this country more than it detracts. That is what we have to weigh. Will the minister tell us what other imports from Finland are affected here, before we go into the exports, besides the kraft paper? There must be something else; I cannot help thinking that if there has been any serious objection from the kraft paper people it must be because the whole information is not given us. Surely in the face of $2,000 of imports as against $3,000,000 of exports there would not be much occasion for worrying about a 4| per cent reduction. There must be more significance to it than appears on the surface.

I will give the imports again, for the ten months ended January, 1925. The first item is cream separators, $2,187. My right hon. friend can figure out for himself what advantage that is going to be to Finland. Cream separators are on our free list. Then there is wrapping paper, kraft, $2,777. On goods from Finland there will be a reduction of 4f per cent.

A little less than $100
altogether.

Canada-Finland Treaty
On tissue paper, same reduction, the value of the import was $3,842; other paper and manufactures, $628.
What about newsprint?

Newsprint is not mentioned.
They do not ship any to Canada.
But they may.

They may, and it will not
hurt anybody if they do. Flagstone, granite, if manufactured, $1,487. The general rate is 35 per cent and the intermediate 32J. We give them a reduction of 2i per cent. All the other articles total $2,660. My right hon. friend can figure out how much Finland is going to get out of this deal.

What is the total volume
of our imports from Finland annually and our exports to Finland?

The total value of the imports for the ten months ended January, 1925, was $13,581, while the total exports to Finland were $908,777. The following were the items of our export to Finland for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1924:
Rye	 $ 173,600
Oatmeal and rolled oats	 66,690
Flour of wheat	 1,322,501
Lard	 67'425
Tires	 7,219
Pipe and tubing	 37,341
Mowing machines	 28,283
Cultivators	 1,510
Other agricultural tools and implements.	699
Ploughs	 2,526
Adding machines	 19,125
Other machinery	 7,820
Automobiles	 13,523
Other vehicles	 3,200
Other articles	 5,817
Total	 $1,754,279
Our total imports during the same period amounted to $6,090.

Is it not possible that we
are importing quantities of Finnish goods through some other country-England, for example? The figures are so vastly different that one would almost think that was being done.
I have no record of that. That would be another question.

Under this resolution we are asked to consider what practically amounts to a treaty of reciprocity with Finland. I am at a loss to know why the government goes all round the world seeking to make trade treaties with all these small countries, while they pass by the one country with whom it is natural we should trade, the United States.
TMr. Crerar.]
What evidence has my hon. friend that the government have not made an attempt to get a treaty with the United States?

When Mr. Fielding brought down the first and second budgets of this parliament, he emphasized the point that we should push for reciprocity with the United States. Since then no member of the cabinet has made any report at all concerning what they have done to bring this about. The United States in many articles are offering us reciprocity. They place on the free list many articles that we produce in Canada, including agricultural implements and boots and shoes. This year, instead of seeking reciprocity with that great country, which is our natural market for many of our products, we have given the United States a slap in the face by increasing the duty on coal.
In answer to the right hon. leader of the opposition, we can classify the consumers of this country, and there is a class of consumers who really have to pay all the unfair charges which unfair tariff measures place against us. For instance, most of these unfair charges are passed on until they come down to the agriculturist, and the market of the agriculturist has been closed in, and no treaty has been made with the United States, which I believe could have been done had we been so minded. There is a country that calls for our store cattle from western Canada. We can raise all the store cattle we like in western Canada on the roughage which is consequent in a grain growing area. In the United States they have the feed and the corn to finish and fatten those beeves, and with the climate as it is, that can be done much more profitably in the United States than with us; but, instead of seeking reciprocity with that great country, which is the natural one for us to trade with, we go all round the world seeking trade treaties with other countries which do not amount to anything; and in all these treaties one thing is noticeable, that organized industry in this country is favoured every time as against the consumer. That class of our population seems to have the ear of the government at all times. To bring the cost of living down does not seem to be the aim of our legislators yet, and until that is done I think any trade treaty is useless while the cost of production and the cost of living in this country remain so high. I think it is a
Canada-Finland Treaty

desirable thing that we should trade with Finland. I am in favour of it, but I think every effort should be bent towards seeking a reciprocal trade arrangement with the country to the south of us.

The minister has referred to the comparatively small total of our imports of kraft paper from Finland. I presume the matter which is troubling the kraft paper manufacturers is that under the proposed reduced tariff the imports will be greatly increased. I think the minister must be aware that the paper mills which produce kraft paper in this country have been having a very hard time. I am informed that one mill in Ontario has closed down altogether because it cannot get a market for its kraft paper.

It so happens that the president, I think, or at all events a director of the kraft mill at Dryden, is one of the men who is urgent that we get this treaty through so that he will he taken care of there in regard to flour.
He is in the flour business too. But the minister says this does not affect flour.

It will, if the United States
gets in.
If!

I have received communications from British Columbia concerns, 'which I forwarded to the minister some time ago. One is from the Westminster Paper Mills. This is a new industry which we expected to be quite an asset to the community as it would employ quite a number of men. I have received a letter from that concern which reads in part as follows:
Understanding that the proposed preferential treaty with Finland, which at the last session was thrown out by the Senate, and under which the duty on kraft wrapping paper imported from Finland into Canada would be reduced from 25 per cent to 20] per cent, we desire to vigorously protest against any reduction in the rate of duty on importations of wrapping paper into Canada, from Finland or elsewhere.

I never said to my right hon. friend that we were getting any concessions in duties. I said very frankly that there was a low duty and there was no preference. The question is on the

Mr. Speaker, I can hardly let this matter come to a vote without stating my position. I understood it had been decided that the amendment should not be moved officially by this group. However, it is now before the House, and some of us in this quarter are placed in a rather awkward position. When the budget was first brought down it was agreed among ourselves that we should move the subamendment, which was in identically the same words as the amendment now before us. The Speaker disallowed the subamendment. His ruling was appealed and I voted against the ruling and in favour of allowing the subamendment. There were then two things before us-the budget and the Conservative amendment. At the time I asked the government some questions respecting certain legislation which I considered was, for this session, just as important to the western people as tariff reductions. Those questions were answered largely in the affirmative, and as a result, not because I agreed altogether with the government policy on the tariff question, but in order to give them an opportunity to bring down legislation , of the character I have referred to, I supported them with my vote. Now once again I am called upon-
Mr. MF.IGHEN:	Will the hon. member
permit a question? Has he any objection to giving the House what it was he asked from the government and what concessions he received?

It was not a matter of concessions at all. I simply said that if the government would outline their policy in regard to the Grain Act and other things,
I was not here with the intention of voting in any particular way in order to get votes; but that I believed the interests of Canada 
were far greater than any question of whether or not people Voted for me. For that reason I supported the budget proposals. At present I am called upon to make a choice between two things, with respect to both of which I have voted affirmatively; and that, of course, makes it very difficult. I might say that the budget passed the House and when it was discussed seriatim a few days ago no one raised any objection to it; that is, there was no vote against it. I cannot vote against the principles expressed in the amendment, and I am not going to swallow myself with respect to the budget. Accordingly, when the vote' is taken on this amendment I intend to leave the House and let the responsibility remain as between myself and my people.

As the hon. member who
has just been speaking (Mr. Lewis) referred to the present amendment having been already before the House as a second amendment to the budget, I wish to state that it was not put by the Chair. It is quite true that I ruled at that time that that amendment could not be moved, 'because on the motion that the Speaker leave the chair for the House to go into committee of Ways and Means on the budget only one amendment can be moved. I allow it now because it is presented on the second reading of the bill bearing on the whole question of supply and ways and means. All authorities agree that on the second reading of such a bill any amendment can be moved which is relevant to the issue. On this point I quote May, twelfth edition, page 357, as follows with regard to the moving of amendments on the second reading of a bill:
It is also competent to a member who desires to place on record any special reasons for not agreeing to the second reading of a bill, to move, as an amendment to the question, a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from, the principles, policy, or provisions of the bill; or expressing opinions as to any circumstances connected with its introduction or prosecution.
But of course it must always be relevant, as it is in the present case. My statement is warranted, because I might be accused of taking one view on one occasion and a different view on another when practically the same question was involved. But on the second reading of a bill like the present one it is proper to seek a remedy for those who have a grievance, on the old principle of the right to air grievances before supply is granted.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before
the House rose a't recess the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans), having reference to the motion that Bill No. 118 be read a second time moved in amendment:
That all the words after the word "that" be struck out and the following be substituted therefor:-
The House regrets that the budget presented by the Acting Minister of Finance countains evidence of the application of unsound principles of public finance, affords no relief from the excessive burdens of indirect taxation and constitutes a failure to carry into effect substantial economies in public expenditure and the fiscal policy of the Liberal party as from time to time enunciated;
And that the policy of protection maintained in the present budget has greatly increased the cost of living and production has failed to provide adequate revenues or to prevent serious depression in trade and industry;
And. be it further resolved that a revision of the tariff schedules, based on the needs for revenue instead of on the principle of protection is long overdue and should be immediately undertaken in order to bring down the costs of living and to place our industries on a permanently sound basis.
As far as I am able to recall, and I think I recall the circumstances correctly, this is the same amendment which the hon. leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) moved at the time the budget resolutions were introduced, and which under the rules of the House it was not permissible to proceed with at that time. Now the hon. member for Saskatoon brings this forward as an amendment to the motion to proceed with the second reading of the bill which is based upon the resolutions that have already passed this House. If any useful purpose could be served in debating a resolution of the kind at this stage, I could understand the motive which has prompted my hon. friend in bringing in the amendment. While it is perfectly true that the amendment when presented by the leader of the Progressive party at the time the budget was introduced could not then be discussed, there is no single affirmation or sentence of the amendment which has not been fully discussed in the course of the long debate which took place on the budget, the longest debate, I think I am correct in saying, which has ever taken place in this parliament, certainly the longest which has ever taken place on the introduction of the budget. Were we to debate the amendment of the hon. member it would only mean spending a lot of time in reiterating arguments and statements which have been discussed at great length for over a period of a month, and
which certainly will not gain any emphasis by being repeated at this time.
I can only say that, under the circumstances, the motion as presented by my hon. friend cannot be construed as other than a motion of want of confidence in the administration. If the amendment were to carry it would mean that the government would not be able to proceed with the business of the country for the reason that it would be deprived of obtaining the revenues essential to the carrying on of the work of public administration. That is the only effect the carrying of this amendment could have.
What is extraordinarily singular is that the bill which the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) is asking the House to permit to have its second reading is in identical terms with the resolutions which were introduced on which it is based, and which passed through the committee stage without a division. That is the feature I would like hon. members of the House to appreciate. The House has already without a single division approved everything of which the government at the present time is asking the House to approve in the bill for which we are now asking a second reading. I am inclined to feel that if my hon. friend the member for Saskatoon had appreciated that such was the significance of his motion, he would possibly-

Might I interrupt my right hon. friend? He states that there was no division of the House on the resolutions on which this bill is based. I would remind the right hon. gentleman that the House was divided on the principle of the resolutions when we divided on the budget; so it can hardly be claimed there was no division.

the silent support and approval of every hon. member of the House. My right hon. friend says that this resolution can have no useful effect. He points out that it cannot have any useful effect because the only thing it could do, if carried, would be to establish a want of confidence in the government. I cannot imagine anything more useful for this Dominion at the present time. If there is any one thing that the people of this country want to-day it is a chance to pronounce upon public questions.
Bring it on.
It is something which would give them an opportunity of saying whether or not the present policy of drift and indecision is to continue.
Go to it!

Hon. gentlemen are exceedingly brave. They have it in their own hands. What is all this bravery about in saying "Go to it"? Who starts it? Who can start the election except the government, unless by some happy chance-
"Chance" is right.

-unless a vote can be passed in this House which will precipitate an election. So that I do not agree at all with my hon. friend in saying that this is an idle resolution having regard for the point from which he attacks it, because, having regard to the point from which he attacks it, it is most useful. The thing that is wrong with this resolution is simply that gentlemen who voted for the budget and voted down another amendment dealing with pressing questions at the present time, namely 
questions of taxation and economy, are now in a position to know that with absolute safety they may vote to turn this government out. That is the weak part, Mr. Speaker, of the situation. There is no question at all as to the facts. Hon. members have framed a resolution in such terms that it puts in somewhat of a quandary any man who has any regard for financial institutions and for the proper progress of the country. Anyone who has a regard for Canada at the present time ought to be trying to get his government out of power, and that same man ought to have and generally does have some regard for the form of the motion submitted to the House. So the situation is perfectly plain. I only speak for myself, but I have to choose between two direct duties, one the maintenance of what I believe to be sound, proper, sane financial proposals, and the other the duty which is an imperative duty that I feel, that I ought to do everything that I can to ensure to the people of Canada the opportunity to register their opinion on the first possible occasion as against this government.
That's that.

An hon. gentleman across the floor had something to say. I did not catch it. What was it? Very good, he had nothing to say. Now on the other hand, Mr. Speaker, this motion can serve a purpose that I do not think is at all commendable. It can serve the purpose of giving my hon. friends to my left the opportunity of voting safely against the government.
My hon. friend can prevent that.

The hon. leader of the Progressive party says we can prevent that. I speak again for myself, and I say I am not in the habit of swallowing my principles for the purpose of making a switch on a vote. I think it is perfectly clear that this resolution has been so drawn as to make it a safety-first resolution, so that some gentlemen will be able to say, "We are opposing the government; we still believe in freer trade. We are against this government; there is our vote," while at the same time feeling assured that that vote is absolutely safe, that nothing is imperilled, and that the vote of want of confidence which ought to be passed by this House is impossible.
I agree with what my hon. friend said that this situation ought not to be made use of for the purpose of entering into another debate. We have already talked a very long time, but I really think my hon. friend went entirely out of his way when he talked about

Customs Tariff
the length of time this House occupied in connection with the budget. The government had it in its hands always to bring the debate to a close, as they brought it to a close when they made up their minds. Further than that, through the whips, my right hon. friend made it known a week before the conclusion. that it was time to bring it to an end. Yet notwitstanding that he went out of his way to castigate the opposition for obstruction.
Order, order.
How am I out of order?

In referring to a former
debate. It is an elementary rule that that cannot be done, and I want a decision on my point of order. We are not going to discuss the budget again.
The hon. gentleman may not know, but I understand this is a continuation of the debate upon that question, and I do not think there is any doubt about it. I await your ruling, Mr. Speaker.

The first motion was for the Speaker to leave the chair for the House to resolve itself into committee of Ways and Means. The resolution went to committee, and was adopted and reported by the committee; two bills were introduced based on the resolution, notably the one we are discussing now. The first reading of the bill was passed, and we are now on the motion for the second reading of the bill. My ruling is that it is the same debate, though at a different stage, and the hon. gentleman is therefore in order.

I felt pretty
sure of my ground on the point of order that was raised. Under these circumstances it ill befits my hon. friend to charge the opposition with obstruction. Hansard itself is the best answer to that allegation. We all know that in parliament when we have not time for preparation, and particularly at the end of a long debate, things are said for which we are sorry afterwards. I admit that at once, but I submit that if there is one person in this world that ought to be careful it is the First Minister of the Crown, and he certainly ought not to make charges of that kind which the records show to be incorrect. So far we have had nothing from my right hon. friend acknowledging his error or pointing out that of all the long speeches delivered on the budget his was the longest.. Yet he makes the charge of Obstruction. I
am not going to give my right hon. friend any opportunity of saying that I am delaying this debate. I simply rose for the purpose of making these few remarks to join with my right hon. friend, not in connection with the major part of his observations, not in connection with that anticipated swan song of his as to what would happen if he could no longer function, but simply as to his one statement that we have had a long debate, a debate which the government could and ought to have stopped long before they did, but did not see their way to do so, and to suggest to hon. members that we ought not to go into another stage of a long debate and that the vote should be taken this evening.

Immigration and Colonization Act

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT

speechtext:
Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Immigration and Colonization) moved the second reading of Bill No. 112 to amend the Department of Immigration and 'Colonization Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 1-Duties and powers of minister.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not
want the minister to think that because we did not oppose the second reading no explanation of this bill is due the committee. We would like to know just exactly what is the purpose of the amendments.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if hon. gentlemen will refer to the exp'anatory notes opposite each section, the amendments will be quite clear to them. The courts of British Columbia gave a decision that section 4 of the Immigration and Colonization Act had the effect of transferring to the Minister of Immigration and Colonization 9 p.m. the power conferred on the Minister of Justice by section 43 of the Immigration Act. The purpose of the amendments is to correct this situation for the future, and to legalize all such orders issued in the past, other than those which have been passed upon by the courts. That is, it is the intention that the Minister of Justice shall deal with all these cases.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Do I understand this has reference to deportation of persons convicted of some criminal offence?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Yes, and who have
served their term.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Will the Minister of Justice kindly explain what is intended?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Apparently, when the
Immigration Act was amended, through some mistake the duty of signing the order for deportation, which had always been done by the Minister of Justice, was unwittingly transferred to the Minister of Immigration. This bill is merely for the purpose of restoring this duty to the Minister of Justice.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am speaking without
preparation, I admit, but I recall some years ago the question of deportation was under discussion, and if my memory does not serve me false, at the time I urged that the Minister of Immigration should deal with the
deportation of persons convicted of felony. Now I am again speaking wholly from memory, but I have in mind we were dealing particularly with offenders under the Narcotic Drugs Act, in which we were very deeply interested on the coast, because at that particular time both there and in Montreal orientals were known to be trafficking in narcotic drugs contrary to the law. The traffic became so notorious that the public of British Columbia was thoroughly aroused, and in order to contribute to the suppression of that illicit traffic it was thought desirable that these traffickers, when convicted, should be deported with very little ceremony; that is, that there should not be too much red tape in the deportation procedure. Having that in view, power was given to the Minister of Immigration to sign the deportation orders. Personally I should like to be very sure that that intention is still to be carried out, and that we are not by this legislation introducing some circuitous procedure. I am not reflecting on the Minister of Justice.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Nor on the Minister of Immigration?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The Minister of Immigration can look after himself in regard to these offenders. The Justice department is supposed to be conducted on a plane somewhat above that of the other departments, and the result is that the Minister of Justice sometimes delays unduly in his consideration of these deportation cases. On the contrary, the Minister of Immigration, acting on the reports of his officers, dealt with them in a more or less summary fashion. I should like to be assured that no greater leniency is to be extended to this class of offenders. This country should desire to get rid of such offenders as quickly as possible. We do not want to throw our courts open to -unlimited appeals from aliens who have been convicted of a felony. Every conviction of an alien should justify our deporting the offender with very little ceremony.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
My hon. friend may be
assured that his remarks will be noted. There is no intention to deal with these men any more leniently. It is simply a question of its being more practical to have this done by the Department of Justice, because the persons to be deported are in the custody of officers of that department.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Will the minister describe the process? What has to be done? Who makes the appeal for the deportation?
3194	COMMONS
Immigration and Colonization Act

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: As I understand it the only object of this act is to give the power to the Minister of Immigration and Colonization, instead of the Minister of Justice, to deport these people.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
No, it is just the
reverse.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Is it thought that the
Minister of Immigration and Colonization is so soft hearted that he cannot do the work, and he wants the Minister of Justice to do it?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is what I am trying to find out.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I think the Minister of
Immigration and Colonization has been doing this work vigorously and with despatch during the last few years. He knows how it has to be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: It has always been done by the Minister of Justice, under section 43 of the Immigration Act. It is the Department of Immigration and Colonization that asks for the amendment so that what has always been the practice shall prevail.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I would like to have a
thorough explanation of this bill. The little conversation that has been going on between the Minister of Justice and the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, with a few words thrown in by the Minister of Immigration, has not made it clear, I am sure, to a good many of us. Will the minister explain it from start to finish?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
It is largely to avoid red
tape. The person who is to be deported is already under the charge of the Minister of Justice and we think it is a slowing down of the process that the necessary documents should first have to go to the Minister of Immigration and Colonization.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Does this deal only with
immigrants coming in, or with persons generally?	_

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
With any person who has
to be deported.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: How many years has a person to be in this country before he is immune from deportation?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Five years, I think.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am a little uneasy
about this legislation, because I recall very well the serious condition which prompted the original legislation. I do not know what influence is demanding this change.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
It is not a change; it .
has always been done in this way. A mere reading of section 43, which is set out in the explanatory notes of the bill, will explain that. The warden of the penitentiary is an officer of the Department of Justice and should receive his orders from the minister of that department.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Is the order for deportation to be issued only at the expiration of the term of the man who is serving the sentence?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Would it not be better to
remove him at once if you are going to get rid of him anyway?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I do not think so. If a
man commits a murder in this country and is sentenced to twenty-five years' imprisonment, he would be very much pleased if we would send him back to Europe instead of detaining him.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The minister's observations make me even more suspicious of this legislation. The minister argues this: "I am the minister in charge of penitentiaries. Here is a statute which authorizes the Minister of Immigration and Colonization to issue an order in respect to a prisoner in one of these institutions. I do not think that is right; the order should be issued by myself." But. here is the weakness of the minister's position: In all sections of the country it is the official of the Immigration department who knows of the case, who is in touch with it, who is watching it. I believe the duty rests upon the clerk of the municipality or the clerk of the court in the municipality or district in which the offence was committed, and where the person to be deported is incarcerated, to notify the Immigration department. The immigration officer gets word of this and it is his business to see to the deportation; in all other forms of deportation these duties are always carried out by an immigration officer. For instance, if an immigration officer finds a person in the country contrary to the immigration law, he has him apprehended, detained, and deported on the next boat.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Who will give the order to the warden of the penitentiary to deliver that man to the officer?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The Minister of Immigration advises the warden-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
There is no connection
between the Minister of Immigration and the warden.

Immigration and Colonization Act

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
We will suppose there
is a man in Vancouver whose day of release is to come to-morrow. The immigration official gets word that to-morrow a certain notorious criminal is to be released. He cannot wire his minister and get an order immediately; it has to go through all the red tape at Ottawa before getting through the Immigration department and the Justice department. If this bill passes I venture to say that hundreds will be released without being detained at all.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That is the difficulty we are
experiencing now: it comes to the Minister of Immigration and the Minister of Immigration sends it to the Justice department; then it goes on to the warden. We propose to shorten the procedure so that it will go direct to the Minister of Justice.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: No. The way it is now-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I have been doing it for the
last three months.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Certainly. The minister
signs the order, and it is immediately communicated to the warden of the penitentiary.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
You are
wrong there.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am not wrong. That
is the law.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The section says so.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is the law; I do not care what circuitous route is followed here. I am objecting for this reason. We had all manner of difficulty in the years preceding 1918 in apprehending particularly violators of the Narcotic Drug Act. It became a veritable scandal on the Pacific coast. Public meetings were held in various cities out there, and in some of the cities eastward, protesting against the laxity of the regulations, the formality involved, and the difficulty of apprehending these people and getting them out of the country. This legislation before us in my estimation wrill make it more difficult than ever to secure the deportation of these individuals who are in the penitentiaries or jails committed for a felony.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Having the Minister of Immigration issue an order to his officer to take charge of the prisoner at the moment he is released did not short cut the thing, and this is not lengthening the process any because in all cases the Minister of Justice had to give the order. To all intents and purposes the prisoner is in charge of the Minister of Justice from the moment of his conviction until his sentence is served, and
the moment the prisoner steps out, instead of the Immigration department executing the deportation, it would be executed by the officer of the Minister of Justice.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Let me ask a question.
At the present time if the Minister of Immigration advises the warden of the penitentiary that such and such a criminal is about to be released and is to be held for deportation, that warden has to hold him.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Certainly, but when you
pass this law and the Minister of Immigration or any accredited officer so advises the warden, the warden says: "No, I take no instructions except from the Minister of Justice," and if it happens that there is a loss of connection between the Immigration department and the Justice department your criminal must be released, and nothing can hold him there. There is no doubt about that. You are simply adding another step to the procedure; that is all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Will not my hon. friend admit that, after all, it is merely a question of procedure? There is no principle involved; it is merely a question of procedure. Now who knows which is the best procedure? Is it not the officers of the departments concerned who have been dealing with this matter for four years, and who have asked that there shall be no change in the procedure which has been followed all this time? Will not my hon. friend admit that after all the officers of the Immigration department as well as the officers of my department should be the best judges of what is the best procedure to follow?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That is a veiy nice way
to put it, but I want to point out to the minister that we have a right to our opinion, and I will say something further to him. I want to tell him it was the failure of both the Justice department and of the Immigration department, not of this government but of past governments, to have a due appreciation of the situation that brought about this legislation in 1918. It was public opinion that forced that legislation on the statute book.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Oh no, it was-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
It certainly was. I had
a good deal to do with it, and this is refreshing my memory. It was the indignation of the public on the Pacific coast that brought about that legislation, and now we are going back to the sleepy methods that were followed in previous days.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Unless I misunderstand this bill, I think a word here is necessary on behalf of the stranger within our gates. I do not understand the member for Vancouver Centre as wishing for more stringent legislation in this regard. If I understand the bill aright, we may detain the immigrant who has committed an offence and keep him in jail or in the penitentiary or reformatory for many years, and then deport him without any further ado. After many years he has lost all connection with the land of his birth, he has lost his standing in this country as well, and we turn him adrift, perhaps penniless. In the name of humanity I think we are dealing too summarily altogether with those who are seeking new homes in our country.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Of course, my hon. friend has read the section of the statute? It applies only to men who are not Canadian citizens or who have not acquired Canadian domicile.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Is it not a fact that those to whom this act would apply mostly require five years' residence in this country before they can obtain citizenship anyway? We may detain that man ten or fifteen years in prison in this country, at the end of which time he has lost all connection with the land of his birth, and then we summarily deport him without trial. It does not seem like British justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: They have not lost citizenship. If a Canadian were to commit a like offence in another country and serve a like sentence, he would come back to Canada as a Canadian citizen. So it works both ways.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Has the minister considered the point raised by the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) as to whether the act could be so amended as to provide for the deportation of these convicts immediately after their conviction instead of keeping them here in the gaol or penitentiaries? It seems to me there might be something in that. I have considered the point previously. As a matter of fact, it has been put up to me by some of the authorities, more particularly in regard to the less serious offences which have resulted in gaol sentences. In the case of a sentence to gaol, what happens? It means that the municipality in which the offence is committed has to maintain the man while he is in gaol awaiting de-
portation. It is very doubtful indeed whether
the confinement in gaol is going to do any of these people any good.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I would draw the hon. member's attention to the fact that section 1 is passed. It is section 2 we are dealing with now, providing that the orders of the Minister of Justice shall be valid.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Section 2 deals distinctly with section 43 of the Immigration Act, which is the one I am discussing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I do not see the
relevancy at the present time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Section 2 distinctly
refers to section 43 of the Immigration Act, and it is that section of the act I am discussing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Is it the hon. member's intention to suggest an amendment to section 43 of the act, as coming within section 2 of this bill? This deals purely with the power of the minister to make an order.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I say that this section is before the committee, and I am discussing with the minister whether it would not be advisable to further consider the suggestion which was made by the hon. member for North Waterloo. If I may proceed, Mr. Chairman-I shall uot be long-when a man is sent to the gaol, the municipality has to pay for his keep until he has served his sentence, and then he is deported. Why not deport him immediately after conviction? I do not see why that could not be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Because he has committed a crime. He has been convicted of a crime and has to serve a sentence. I am sure my hon. friend would be very popular with these people if, under such circumstances, he would allow them all to go scot-free.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Suppose two men, one a Canadian and one an American citizen, commit a crime. The Canadian would be sen-, fenced to two years in the penitentiary for his offence, while the American would be sent to New York, both having committed the same offence. The thing is absurd on the face of it. The man should be punished, and in addition to that he should be sent out of the country. But to sentence a man to repatriation for an offence would make the Minister of Justice most popular with alien criminals. Suppose a man wants to go back to London and. has not the means; he says to himself, "I will commit an offence, incur

Dominion Lands Act
imprisonment for two years, and be sent back to my country, without any cost- to myself." Such a procedure would be placing a premium on crime.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: In the meantime, if you do not do that, you are simply providing him with board and lodging, because a man who is so unprincipled as to endeavour to do what has been suggested by the hon. member lor George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) would not care very much whether he was kept in gaol or not. This provision for the deportation of a foreigner who has committed an offence in this country is comparatively recent. When you send a man to the penitentiary what happens? The government has to keep him there and educate him.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Where would New Westminster be if you did not have a penitentiary.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I guess it would be in the same place as it is now. The government has to keep and educate this man and all that kind of thing, and the difference to my mind is this, that we owe a duty to Canadian citizens and British subjects, but we do not owe any duty to foreigners. When we deport them we are inflicting upon them possibly the greatest penalty that we can impose

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
My hon.
friend suggests that we owe a duty to British subjects coming here on our solicitation, but that we do not owe any duty to foreigners Does he really mean that, or is that just a joke? I really do not think the hon. member can be serious in that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: We apparently do not owe any duty to the people who are not Canadian subjects when we throw them out of the country. When we deport them we are through with them and they cannot come back to Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: But we are not paying them a compliment either by keeping them in gaol.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
But we are going to a lot of expense in keeping them in gaol, and the question is whether we should do that or not. I am simply suggesting this to the minister as something that might be considered. I do not say that I am absolutely in favour of it. I can quite see that lawyers might cast it aside as being ridiculous, but at the same time the more I think of it the more I am convinced that this matter should receive some consideration.
Mr. H.OEY: Will the minister tell us if all such prisoners after release are deported, or are exceptions made in certain cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF IMMIGRATION AND COLONIZATION ACT AMENDMENT
