The House resumed from May 11, consideration in committee of Bill No. 75, to amend the Dominion Lands Act.-Hon. Mr. Stewart (Angenteuil)-Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On sectiom 1-Conditions of entry for lands in Saskatchewan and Alberta south of south boundary of township 16.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is
just the one clause in this bill dealing with the sale of school lan|ds, and it was not finished when we were m committee the other day.

*9
Dominion Lands Act
The hon. member for East York (Mr. Harris) moved an amendment, and I asked time to consider it. I have now drafted a proviso that will cover the objection taken by the hon. member. This proviso reads:
And provided that no action shall be taken save and in respect of a holder who has been actually fanning such lands in a proper and husband-like manner.
That is in order to take in onlly the men who are actually farming these lands, not the speculator who is using these lands for speculative purposes. This provision has been copied from the form of mortgage describing cultivated land. I have adopted the same clause and embodied it in this section. It amply covers the objection raised by hon. gentlemen opposite.
What is meant by "such lands"? Does that mean lands that are surrendered or lands or quarter sections that are to be retained or the whole of the land bought?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It means
that the lands in question, whatever lands they are, both those that are surrendered and those to be retained, are being farmed. The idea is not to allow the speculator to come in who is not farming the lands, who is holding them for speculative purposes. Frankly, I do not think there are any left, but I tried to meet the objection so that this will be confined to men who are actually carrying on farming operations on those lands.

A man might have
bought at a school land sale a section of land and he might be fanning only a quarter of it. He desires to retain that quarter and to abandon the other three quarters. He could not do that under this amendment. He would have to' be actually farming the whole section. My point is this, that under the amendment as worded, I fear the minister virtually negatives the whole clause. What I mean is this:	No man who is farming
land which he has bought at a single sale, will be anxious to give up that part of the land which he has under cultivation.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If my right hon. friend is speaking of farming, say 160 acres, no one farms the whole 160 acres. He farms portions of that. What I am trying to avoid is to say that, without his having performed any duties upon the land, he would be entitled to give it up.

What the minister means is this, that if a man is farming a portion of the actual land bought, that should be 
sufficient. The way in which the minister has this worded, the mam would have to be farming in a good and husbandlike manner, perhaps not every acre, but every portion. I presume the minister means-and if he does, he is right-that even a man who is living in a town, provided that he is farming the land by means of a tenant or an employee, is entitled to the relief just the same as anybody else.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, if he is spending money on the property.

I think that is quite
proper, but I fear the minister's wording will have to be extended; otherwise, it will mean that the man has to be farming every portion of the land even though he is not ploughing every portion of it. Any man who is doing that is not going to give up the rest and have all his payments centre on the one quarter.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
All I am
seeking to avoid is that the speculator should come in and take advantage of this provision We want simply to deal with men Who can prove to the satisfaction of the department that they are in a position where they cannot continue; that they are liable to sustain serious loss, and that they have been putting forth their best endeavours to farm the land. They are the people whose investment we are trying to save. If a man is in no danger of losing his investment, he has no cause for complaint and he cannot ask to be taken under the protection of this legislation. Cases, however, constantly come to our notice of the kind I have described. There is a case on the Bluckfoot reserve of a couple who have spent 830,000 in trying to develop a farm. The husband died a year ago. The widow is left in possession of the property and she is unable to carry it on. There is no section in the Indian Act that gives me authority to deal with that case, but it is identical with cases that arise. The land which this couple have been farming comprises a considerable acreage. I have forgotten the quantity. So far as I am able to ascertain, they have been fanning it in a good, husbandlike manner, but the widow has got into a position where it is impossible for her to carry on. If she could surrender part of the land and apply the payments on the balance, that would get her out of a very difficult situation. That is exactly how I mean to apply this provision. I have gone carefully into this question, and I think the clause is drafted so as to give, us authority to deal with these cases where they arise.

Dominion Lands Act

Supposing a man buys a section and sells half of it, and the purchaser who buys on an agreement of sale, cultivates a portion of that. The man is not farming anj of it at all, but he has some of it under cultivation through his purchaser. He applies to have the moneys he has paid all devoted to the redemption of the half section that he has sold. Will the minister feel that he is empowered under this amendment to yield to the importunities of that man?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Do I understand my right lion, friend to suggest that the other half the man is holding himself would not be cultivated?

Yes. He bought it all
as one piece.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
He could
scarcely claim to apply the payments on the half that was uncultivated to the half that was cultivated. That is one of the very serious difficulties with which we have to contend. The method of disposing of these lands by agreements of sale creates endless difficulties in making adjustment. There are so many parties interested in the matter that it almost puts an adjustment beyond the bounds of possibility.

Supposing
one of these parcels of land to which the right hon. gentleman has called the minister's attention were used simply as grazing land for grazing purposes, and the other portion is the portion of which the minister has spoken, that is cultivated. The man is in difficulties. What is there in this legislation to prevent that man from having the payments on both quarters apply on the cultivated one and so get out from under his liability on the uncultivated land?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
One can
hardly conceive of the various angles that will arise in connection with dealing with a question of this kind; but the legislation is devised, so far as we can devise it, for the purpose of meeting cases of real distress. I am not tying them down to just how much cultivation there shall be or whether it shall be fifty, sixty or seventy-five acres. If a man had a half section that he wished to retain without any cultivation on it, I would hesitate to some extent. If it were a quarter section, that would be a different matter, and I think I could agree to that, provided that he had a half section well cultivated and was having difficulty in meeting his payments.

What would happen in a case where a whole section, say of school land, purchased by a settler residing near there, was grazing land, was purchased for that purpose and he got into difficulties in just the same way as a man who bought land for farming and was unable to carry it on? Would the same treatment apply to him? Could he surrender three-quarters and keep one?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am sorry, but we do not cover that case. The moment you do that, you immediately cover the case of land with a two-strand wire fence around it, leased by a speculator for somebody to graze his stock upon. That is, perhaps, a real difficulty and it may be somewhat of a hardship. But if you carry it to that extent, the other purchaser comes in with whom we do not wish to deal.

I am sure the minister
will agree with me that there are some cases where this land is not leased, but purchased solely for that purpose, because pasture is scarce in some of those sections in the west. It might in a few cases work a hardship on such a man.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I had a fairly wide experience in this matter before coming here. We encountered all sorts of difficulties and I made some trips to Ottawa with regard to the leasing of school lands held by speculators or by people who hoped for an increase in value by leasing the land for a time. The real reason these people leased the land in our province was to get out of the wild land tax; and they avoided this by putting stock on the land. We were forced to meet this attempt to avoid taxation by enacting a clause providing that the stock must be the bona fide property of the owner of the land. If we undertook to assist cases of the kind suggested we might step into difficulties of all sorts. It was to meet the objection raised in the committee on the previous occasion that I drew up the clause I am now suggesting.
The minister is going to be in a position under this amendment to do pretty much as he likes.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is
true.

And I do not know how the amendment could be framed to avoid putting him in that position. I want to put myself on record to this effect: This legisla-

Dominion Lands Act

tion will result in bringing back into the title of the government a very large proportion of the outstanding school land sales. The title will revert to the department and not only will the progress which has been made in school land sales for many years be arrekted, but retrogression to a great extent will ensue. I ask the minister to note what I am saying now; he will find that this will be the result.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot
share the fear expressed by my right hon. friend. We know pretty well now the number of rescissions that will take place. We have had a great deal of correspondence and the matter was discussed fully with the provincial governments before this ktep was taken. It will be applied only in cases where there is real distress. It is true, as my right hon. friend says, that considerable power is placed in the hands of the minister, and this is necessary if the act is to be practicable.
Approximately, what is the amount of the arrears on school lands?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I could not give that information now; I will submit it when the estimates are under consideration.

This will be an expedient to relieve the large purchaser to a very great extent; he is the beneficiary of this legislation. But the small purchaser cannot possibly be relieved at all. The fellow who bought a quarter section in the boom times at a high figure must make his payment or lose his money; but the man that bought a section or two, if he is farming part of it, can come to the foot of the throne and make out a case for a lease. The poor chap with a quarter section must stay with his bargain.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Very few
fail on the quarter section. I do not think, speaking from memory, that I have one application from an individual who has purchased a quarter section.

What could the poor
fellow apply for? There is no smaller unit; he has to stick, that is all.

Does the department allow the purchaser of school land to re-sell the land to a second party? If so, does the department hold the original purchaser good for the full payment in case the second purchaser does not come through?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
quite follow the question.

I want to know whether
purchasers of school lands are allowed to resell, and, in that case, whether the department holds the original purchaser good for the amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In most
cases the sales are made by agreement, and the great difficulty in the department is that frequently it is not notified. But if they are prepared to pay out the amount against the land then the first purchaser is released, but not until the amount is paid.

The minister I think has missed the point. What the hon. member wants to know is whether the department can hold responsible the person who purchases from the government's vendee. He cannot be held responsible, nor can the government hold their own purchaser responsible, inasmuch as the government's purchaser does not enter into any agreement at all; he gets a receipt for the money he pays. It amounts to this, that the purchaser from the government really takes rn option, but he is not bound personally; there is nothing by which he can be made to pay a cent. All he suffers is the loss of the first, payment in case he does not come through.
On -the other hand, by that policy the government it seems is in a favoured position to cancel the land not held by legal restriction.
That is right.

In the past I think the department has erred on the side of leniency. A great deal of this land passes into the hands of speculators and is turned over by them to bona fide farmers at a large price. The speculator's object is to secure all the equity he can from the farmer. The farmer in many cases has broken up the land, he has put his buildings on it, having done all the work of development, and now he finds that the payments have not been kept up to the department; in fact, in some cases that I know of nothing further than the original payment was made. The farmer on the land wants possession of it and cannot secure it. I think the policy of the government should be to eliminate the speculator and eliminate him immediately; but in a great many cases they are not doing so. It is in cases where the land was purchased by wealthy men that the government is extending the most protection to the speculator. I know of instances in which land was bought at from six to eight dollars per acre originally and was turned over to the farmers at as high as

Dominion Lands Act
eighteen dollars. A farmer has worked on it for years, having spent a lot of money, and now he finds he has no opportunity of securing it. The speculator never paid any taxes and the farmer has let his own taxes run on, because he did not know whether he would acquire the land or not. The municipalities were not able to collect the taxes for the reason that there was no title to the land and they did not want to seize from the farmer; they knew he had his share of the crop to deliver to the original purchaser and they feared to put him out of business. The result is that the taxes have run up in arrears to an enormous extent; in one case I know of there is nearly $1,000 against one particular quarter section. A municipal officer told me some time ago that in view of the trouble they have experienced they would prefer to lose the taxes if they can eliminate the first party. It seems to me that if the department would wipe out the speculator and get the bona fide farmer on the land the municipalities could secure their taxes and be in better shape than they are to-day, because they would be doing business direct with the farmers. The only thing for the minister to do is, as I say, to eliminate the speculator, who has been a curse to western Canada. With regard to the -question raised by the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Meighen), that a man might be living in a town and yet be farming his land by proxy, there are a great many cases of that kind and these men might be entitled to consideration. In many cases it has happened that some man has gone on the land and worked on it a very short time and then moved in town to engage in some other business, and necessarily he had to rent the land or get someone else to work it. In that case I would say that the man would be entitled to consideration, but I think the minister should not be bound by any very definite legal restriction and that he is perfectly right in leaving the matter to his own judgment. Indeed, I do not think it can be handled any other way. But I should like to point out that in the case of a speculator, who never intended to farm the land, but just used it to farm the farmer, merely trying to get all the money he could out of it without doing any work, and in a good many cases where he did not sell it had some broken up to comply with the provisions of the Wild Lands Act. I think the minister should take drastic action and eliminate that speculator. I want to point out another feature, that in re-selling the land the man residing on it should have the first opportunity to purchase.
205i
There are some cases of very great hardship, and in the cases I have referred to I may say that the department has been very fair and always willing to give the man on the land the first opportunity to purchase. I think that should be borne in mind, that somebody else might step in and put up a little more cash or pay a few dollars more and the man on the land would be losing his equity and forced out on the road.

How does the minister
feel about that speculative argument?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The speculator is very hard to eliminate. When you attempt to do so you wipe out the purchaser too. You cannot do anything in that case. If he has made a sale of the property, and the property is cultivated, we cannot be responsible for the collection of the taxes. Where you find a speculator in possession of land to-day, he is paying the interest, although he may not .'be paying any of the principal. When he gets in arrears with his interest payments we take action; not so when the mani in arrears is the actual farmer. But if that speculator has some other man on the land working it, then you are going to put the latter out of business as well as the speculator the moment you take action on the contract. My hon. friend may say: Well, is there not some process by which you can protect the man on the land? There is not, because under the act we must sell the land by auction.

I think the minister has missed the point of my argument. We will say a speculator bought land at ten dollars an acre, and resold it at fifteen dollars an acre to a farmer. His object is not to pay the original amount to the department at all, but as quickly as possible to secure his equity, and then assign what equity he may have to the farmer on the land. If the minister cares to look up the figures in his department he will find that m a great many cases the interest payments are not being kept up. I understand the minister has nothing to do with payment of the taxes, but I think the department is under a moral obligation to the municipalities to at least be reasonable in the matter. The point is this, the speculator should be eliminated and the land, or a reasonable amount of it, resold to the man on it. In most cases this man might be ahead by this proceeding, because he probably bought that land at a time when the value of it was inflated above what it is worth today. In a good many cases the speculator
Dominion Lands Act

never secured his full equity because the value of the land has dropped to such an extent that it is probably not more than equal to the amount of the original purchase price and any accrued interest there may be. In that case it would be perfectly fair to sell the land to the farmer. You would not be putting him out of business as the minister suggested; you would ibe putting him in business, because he would prefer to deal with the department rather than with the speculator. He would at least knory where he stood, and in a great many cases he would be getting the land a little cheaper than the amount that is against it to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am sorry,
but it cannot be done.

Is not every quarter section
a separate sale? And in case a man bought ten quarter sections at one of these school sales, and is now farming three or four of these quarter sections, would he be able to turn them back under this suggested amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, he would
not, I can assure you.
If he could not turn back those extra quarter sections, -where would you put the limit?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If he is only farming one or two quarter sections, and is doing nothing with the balance but grazing them, he would not be entitled to consideration. Right off the bat I would say so.

If the member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) is right-and I fancy he is, from recollection

that each unit is a quarter section, what is the effect of the minister's amendment? The land referred to in the minister's amendment cannot be any of the land except the land in the one sale.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If he is
farming the land in a good and husbandlike manner-
What land?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The land he purchased; and he has purchased twenty, ten or two sections-
Quarter sections.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. But he is the owner of ten or fifteen quarter sections, and the mere fact that because the sale was made for one quarter section does not limit the action provided for by the amendment.
[Mr. Campbell. |
Suppose a man has bought ten quarter sections, does the minister mean he might actually be farming in a good and husbandlike manner the whole ten quarter sections?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

What does he mean?
That is what he said before.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
True; but
surely my right hon. friend wou'd not expect that the act would so provide? We would much rather have not touched it if that were the case and left it absolutely to the jurisdiction of the minister; but we are trying to throw some protection around the minister as to how he shall deal with these sales.
What is the meaning?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The meaning is that farming operations shall have been carried on in a good and husbandlike manner.
On how much land?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I did not put in the acreage, because if I did so it would probably nullify the effect of the whole thing. You have to leave that to the discretion of the minister. But when you ask me if I am going to cancel eight or ten quarter sections of uncultivated land for one individual, I answer, certainly not.

The minister cannot get through the maze so easily. Here he has an amendment which says that he cannot apply this relief clause unless the purchaser of, say ten quarter sections, is farming that land in a good and husbandlike manner. When I asked him what that " land '' meant, he said the land bought. I do not see
10 p.m. how it could mean anything e'se.
That is, he must be farming the ten quarter sections in a good and husbandlike manner, he must be farming each of them; there is no other way to farm them; he cannot farm every acre of each of them. Under the law he will have to be farming each of these ten quarter sections.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, no; my right hon. friend has missed that.
I have not missed it. The minister told me that.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

The minister's answer
was quite right; I have just read the amendment through. Under the amendment as he has it he would be powerless to apply the relief

Supply-Trade and Commerce
unless the applicant was farming each of the quarter sections in a good and husbandlike manner. Any man who is actually farming the land is not going to ask that the contract be cancelled.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My right
hon. friend is wrong there. I know of at least a dozen half sections, in respect of which applications are now in the office, where 75 per cent of the lands are being farmed.
Oh, yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
And the
request comes to have the purchase price applied on the one quarter.

That is, one quarter of
the half?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, 75 per
cent of the whole is being farmed, and they want to give up one quarter and apply the payments on the other. Many men who are farming on half sections owe more than the original purchase price, to say nothing of what they have paid in, and these are the real cases of hardship. It will help them out very materially if we apply the payments on the one quarter section and release them in respect to the remainder. There are not many men with eight or ten quarter sections in these days; those are mostly all cancelled.

The minister is perfectly correct in his summing up of the case. I know of a man who bought a half section of school land around 1917 or 1918 and has since been farming practically the whole of it, with the exception of a little pasture. He put up substantial buildings on one quarter- house, barn, stables, granaries-and had a well dug and fencing built. At the time he bought the land there wag great inflation of land values and possibly he paid too high a price; and he has been unable to keep up with the payments on the half section. So that to-day he is in the position of having made very substantial payments on the half section but of being unable to make good on the whole of his land. This legislation will enable him to release one quarter back to the department and have a chance to make good on the other quarter. This is not the only case of the kind. These men unwisely bought at an inflated value more land than they could handle, and they now find that after two or three years labour they are faced with the loss of everything because they cannot make good their payments.

The minister stated
that the suggestions I made to him could not be carried out. I am quite aware that they could not be carried out in connection with school lands, but I was speaking in a general way of all government land. As a matter of fact I had particular reference to Indian land, of which the department can make direct sales after the original purchase has been cancelled. That is really what I had in mind, and perhaps I should have explained that to the minister. There is an enormous amount of land under the control of the Indian department which was. sold to speculators, the payments having been in arrears, in some cases only the original payments having been made.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

Did the minister say the
Bridge River Power Company?
The Bridge River Power Company applied for and received a license to export 28,000 kilowatts.

They have not got a
plant yet.

and paid the fee.

This is rather a serious
thing. I am quite certain that the Bridge River Power Company have no plant. I am certainly very derelict in my duty in attending to the development in my province if they have. Why should1 a company without a plant to export get a license to export 28,000 kilowatts? Does the minister give a license to a firm that has not got power to export?

My deputy informs me they
complied with the law. I do not know whether the application was renewed this year, but they made application last year for a license and complied with the law.

I am going to ask the
minister if he would be good enough to lay on the table a full copy of the correspondence and the license in regard to it.
I shall be very glad to comply with that request.

That brings me to this
very important question, and that is the export of power. This would indicate

and I wish the Prime Minister and other ministers would take note of this; I do not say it id any critical sense at all, I am very earnest about it-this would indicate what naturally a person looking purely for monetary advantage will tend to do. that is, to secure some privilege or right, then make contracts on the other side for the sale of that power. Here is a firm, for instance, that I am certain has no plant at all. They apply for and receive a license as if they were going to export. Naturally the only assumption you can make is that they then go to the other side of the line and make contracts for the purchase of power, then come back here and say to financiers: "We have a license to export, we have contracts on the other side for the purchase of power, and now we want financing for the erection or completion of a plant." Now what does that mean? It means the gradual establishment south of the line of a vested right in the power,. of a contractual character. I want to say to the government this: In my estimation, if we allow this process to go on, the result is going to be that there will be established in certain places south of the line factories, and small towns built up around those factories, with certain vested interests there dependent upon the receipt of this power, which they

Supply-Trade and Commerce
will claim later on was contracted for in perfect good faith. Then it will become a question of dispute between the two governments as to whether or not that power can be cut off.
I am going to repeat what I said in the budget debate. ' Power ought to be looked upon as an implement, a tool, and not as a product, and I think we should serve notice to the world that we expect persons who want our power to put their factory beside the power. That is what I think we ought to do. I will admit that if you can eliminate altogether all danger of the establishment of a vested right, then perhaps when you have a surplus of power during the period of development in this country, it is not a bad thing to sell power; I am not disputing that. But let us take this Carillon development, this big concern that desires a power development contiguous to this district. What is the desire there? The desire is to establish on a hydro-electric site a big power plant, ostensibly and deliberately with the intention of exporting power from that plant. The whole undertaking has that in mind. Now if the government say to the Carillon Power Company just as they have said to the Bridge River Company: "Yes, we will give you a license to export," and then the company go on and put in what they represent as $25,000,000 or something of that kind, secure $25,000,000 or $30,000,000 of American capital and invest it in that plant; and then they commence to export. A little later on, perhaps five years from now, the people of Ontario and Quebec will say: "We want power." There comes a big demand for power, and the price of power goes up. They turn to the Carillon Power Company and say: "You are exporting all your power. Why not sell some in Canada?" "Oh," they will say, "we got this power five years ago from the Dominion government with the distinct understanding that we were going to export. It is true the license was to be renewed from year to year, but the government and the people of Canada knew this power was for export purposes." Then they will point to the vested rights south of the line that have been established because of that right to export.
I want to warn the government, and warn the country, that this whole policy that is gradually growing up and becoming established ought in my estimation to be abandoned. I think the world ought to be informed that so far as Canada is concerned, hydro-electric power is looked upon as an implement or tool for the purpose of serving the factories of Canada, and that we invite industries to come to the power; but we warn
them we are not going to adopt or follow a policy of exporting power to industries in a foreign country.
Take the export of power on the Pacific coast. There are two companies, now one -the Western Canada Power and the B.C. Electric, two most estimable companies; I am not criticizing them at all. They are exporting power. Then, here is the Bridge River Company coming along, desirous of promoting a plant, and within a very few years, with the expansion clearly in sight in that country, there will be a demand for all the power that can be obtained. Take Vancouver City, which is dependent on the B.C. Electric and the Western Canada Power Company at the present time. I venture to say that the expansion of the city of Vancouver continuing in the ratio of the last five years will result inside of ten years in the absorption of all the power available at the present time. Now supposing at the end of ten years, or even five years, this increase is commensurate with what I have intimated; what is going to result? The B.C. Electric and the Western Canada Power Company are bound to say: "The price must go up. We cannot supply our customers south of the line with whom we have contracts, and we cannot increase the sale here. We have a demand for all the power we can produce." Then what will be the result? The retarding of the development of industry on the Canadian side. On the other hand, if we discourage the export of this .power, then there would be evidence on the part of Canadian hydro-power companies to develop industries in the neighbourhood in order to take all the power they could develop. In other words, you put pressure on the development otf industry in Canada, whereas under the present policy we are virtually putting a premium on the export of power, and a retarding influence upon the development of industry in Canada.
I do not desire to delay the committee at any length because it is late, but I want to make myself abundantly clear. I consider this question of the export of power, if not the most important, one of the most important questions before parliament to-day or that has been before parliament this year or last year or for many years. I believe in its effect in the future it will be found to have far greater significance than we at the present time dream of. I saw a statement the other day which I cannot quote exactly, intimating however that we could not absorb the power that is possible of development in Canada over long periods of years.

On the other hand, I am advised by those who understand the business-and I had hoped to have here to-night definite data on this, but I have not-that in a definite period of time, some ten or fifteen years, or some twenty years, we will, in Ontario and Quebec, reach the limit of power. That is making a very broad statement and I was surprised to hear it. So that when we hear these statements I think it behooves the government of Canada to be very, very careful. Notice should be served at once on all these companies the minister has cited that they must not consider these licenses as in any sense constituting a guarantee that they would be continued next year, or at any future time, with of course the exception of those that are under contract under some regulations of the past, and I understand there are only a very few small contracts existing.

positive guarantee, but I have been trying to point out to the minister-and I hope he will not think I am doing it in a critical spirit-that it is a question which has obtruded itself on parliament this session. But I come back to the Carillon case, and I tell my hon. friend now that if this government were to give to the Carillon Power Company a license to export, as he has done the Bridge River Company, on the strength of that contracts would be made south of the line, 325,000,000 of capital would be supplied, the plant would be established on that understanding, and then later on the Carillon Power Company would say to this government or its successor, "Why, we advised you at the time, you knew what we were doing and here is a vested interest." The government of the United States would probably take the same view. It would become immediately a matter between the governments, and I think we know from a study of history that the moment a thing becomes a matter between governments it is very difficult of solution or of being easily unravelled. Regarding the Caril-

Ion Power Company, I think the Dominion of Canada should hesitate-not only hesitate, but I think should refuse-to be tied in any sense by any inferential guarantee, not a definite written guarantee but an inferential guarantee, to the Carillon Power Company or any other company, and that they should do more than that, and should serve notice on the world that these annual licenses are in every sense of the term temporary licenses, and that the purpose of Canada in the future is to retain the power for the development of Canadian industry.

I had a letter today from the mayor of Toronto drawing my attention to this matter. He said that he had protested to the government in regard to certain contracts that had. been made in the past in connection with hydro-electric development and in which a lot of the municipalities of Ontario were interested, and that the consequence of this export duty on power going out of the countiy would be to put a load on the municipalities which have gone into the business and let the contracts in the past to American companies at a very low rate. They have a proposition before the government now, I understand, that they at least be relieved from the export tax by reason of these contracts made some years ago, and in regard to that I should like to know whether the government has any intention of taking into consideration the protest of Toronto and associated municipalities in this matter. I agree with what the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) has stated, and I want to say that the HydroElectric 'has now under consideration the establishment of a large steam plant in Toronto for the generation of power to supplement the production of hydro electric power.
Ten million dollars.

Yes, ten million dollars. That is going on in other directions, and there is a great famine of power in almost immediate prospect. I spoke on this question the other day, and I said, "Our greatest resource to-day is the generation of power on our great rivers north to the Hudson hay slope". They will probably jointly produce millions of harse-ipower. Science is going ahead so rapidly in the way of high tension wires and long distance transmission, the products of those rivers will be worth millions and millions to us, and we ought to start now and say that not one kilowatt of that power shall go out of the country if it can be kept here. It might be an immense source of revenue. If we have a transporta-

tion problem ahead of us, as apparently we have, and the 'cost of teansjportation is a most vital matter in connection with industry, we ought to keep that power for transmission purposes and not let it go out of the country. That would be the solution of .this tremendous problem more than anything eilse. I say to my hon. friends from the west that they ought to put in a protest now if they wish to keep down transportation 'charges. But if we start now and make cOmimitmente in which Americans will be interested and will be able to go to their government anid allege unfair .treatment on the pant of Canada, we will -be embroiled with the American people, and the firms which make the contracts, so that I join with my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre in saying we should call! a halt now and .that there should be no commitment in regard to any of 'the privileges. I .ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) if he has heard of the protest made by the City of Toronto that this export tax should not apply to thorn in connection with the contracts made years ago with the Hydro-Electric. If we do as I have suggested we will get a new national (pdlicy in this country in connection with power. The .greatest asset we have .to-day is the immense power we have in our country, and if we sit quietly by, those who see the large profits in exporting it, will foe laying plans to get control of it, and they will entrench .themselves so that it will be very hard to dislodge them.
I again urge on 'the government-and I hope our friends from the west will make the same appeal to them-to call a halt in connection with the export of something which we have got which is limited ini quantity, because it will pass out of our hands if we do not guard ourselves.

Without any invitation from my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) I intend to say a few words on this matter. I listened to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, .and it seems to me the arguments he advanced are worthy of ithe most serious iconsidteratiion on the part of ithe minister. I can easily see how, by our exporting power, large factories being built and villages and towns growing up around those factories in the future, this .may became, as has already 'been said, an international question. I do not think there is much 'danger of the prairie provinces exporting any water-power to the United States.
That will come in five years. There is the Nelson river.

Yes. I believe some day we shall have on the Nelson river perhaps the 206
greatest water-power in Canada. I have been impressed by the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, and this question should be gone into very carefully in order to ensure that no vested interests are created .that will cause international trouble. There is no doubt the time is coming when Canada will use all her water-power. It seems almost foolish in a way that water running down, which is of no use at the present time, which will continue to flow for all time .and which is not a thing that can be used up, should not be used by some people who can take advantage of it at the present time. Still, the argument has been advanced that if you give the power away to a foreign country, it may be difficult afterwards to restore things to their original condition. This question ought to receive the most careful attention and consideration before commitments are entered into that we may regret in the future.

I had not the pleasure of being in the House when this discussion began, but I should like in a very few words to take issue with what has been said by the father of the House Mr. Maclean, (York), who has not shown in this regard that broad, generous, far-sighted spirit which usually characterizes his utterances. The idea that we in Canada, with 90 per cent of our electrical power undeveloped, should not use that vast potential power by turning it into electrical energy so that it might be exported and help us to pay our debts, is, I think, perfectly preposterous nonsense. The hon. gentleman will pardon me if I have said anything unparliamentary. We have in Quebec, I am told about 14,090,000 horsepower and we have developed about 1,000,000 horse-power. The suggestion is that we should leave that 13,000,000 horse-power undeveloped because in years to come we may want it for ourselves.
That is not the suggestion at all.

That is the suggestion because, if you are going to prohibit its export and there is no market for it at home, how will it be developed? It will not be developed unless it can be used, and if it cannot be used in this country, it cannot be used unless it be exported.
I would like to suggest to my hon. friend that he is the one that is talking the preposterous nonsense now.

That is a matter of opinion. I used to think our protectionist friends were anxious to see an increase in the

exports of this country, and that the idea of imports into this country caused them alarm. Usually they were always anxious for a favourable balance of trade and they rather encouraged exports. If we can manufacture power and sell it abroad when we cannot use it at home, surely we should be allowed to do so.

Can the hon. member see a way clear that at any time Canada, after allowing that power to be exported for a number of years can say: Now, this must stop; we need this power for ourselves? Can that be managed all right?

Without any doubt.
Mr. FOlRKE: It is all right if that can be done.
Mr. MoMA'STER: First of all, water-powers should never be sold. They should be leased to companies, and one of the conditions of the lease should be that the first charge upon the company, so far as their customers were concerned, would be to see that Canadian customers were supplied.	If there was
not enough to go around, Canadian customers must have the preference.	As
power would get more valuable and expensive, the market for it inside the country would develop, and there would be no question but that regulations could be made to preserve for Canadian use such portions of the power as were necessary for Canadian use. The point I want to make is this, that we have in this country vast sources of potential electrical power which, if it can be turned to account and exported, it would be wise and in the interest of the country to export.
There is another phase of the situation. How can we, with any common sense, play the dog in the manger on this continent? How can we say, with wisdom or even with safety: We have sources of power which we will not allow you, our American cousins, to use, even on terms fair to ourselves, because in the far distant future we may possibly need it ourselves. Supposing the United States followed the same policy with us, where would we be? I saw the other day that the Premier of Ontario said: If American manufacturers want to use our electrical power, let them come into Ontario and manufacture in Ontario.
Or in Quebec.

In Canada, let us say
In what position would the textile manufacturers be if the United States said:	If you

That is different. One is
a raw material and the other is an implement.

Power would be manufactured in Canada and' sent into the United States. Cotton would foe grown in the United States and sent into Canada. A policy of restriction in this country is extremely unwise. I trust to hear less in this House and elsewhere of that narrow and unwise policy of closing the walls of Canada against the export of power or anything else.

Can the minister give us a little more 'information in regard to this Bridge River Power Company? Who is the president of this company? Who is the secretary? What is the capitalization? What is the capital that has been paid in? What are the conditions under which a license has been issued? Is it an American or a Canadian concern?

I am very sorry I have not
the information here to-night, but I shall be glad to give it to my hon. friend to-morrow or at any other time. I am now trying to find out by telephone just when this license was first granted to the Bridge River Power Company. If the information comes before we adjourn, I shall be glad to give it to my hon. friend.
As regards the discussion on the export of power, I quite agree with the hon. member for Vancouver Centre that it would be a splendid idea if we could force these industries to come to this country and establish here. But after all, there is another side to the question. The water is, as some hon. member has remarked, flowing away. In other words, dollars are flowing by. The question we must adk ourselves! is: Are we to allow these dollars to flow away from us for the next twenty or twenty-five years until such time as the industries are ready to establish in this country? With our mineral wealth it is different; if we do not take it out of the ground to-day it will be there to-morrow. But the water that flows by to-day we shall not be able to use to-morrow, and millions of dollars in the next twenty-five years might come to the country through the export of power. Most industries in Canada require some export business; I know that the industries with which I am connected always require an export trade. We are able to sell 75

per cent of our output in this country but we want the balance in the way of export trade to keep the wheels of the factories running day and night. And power is much the same.
No.

Power may remain idle for
years unless there is some use for it at home, and if we are able to export a small quantity of it, above what is necessary for home purposes in the locality in which it is developed, it is possible to develop a valuable business in the interests of our people. This year, before a license was granted, I notified all exporting companies that before we would renew any licenses they would have to submit to the department a declaration that the power was not required at home and that there was ample power to supply all the needs in the locality in which it was developed.
So far as vested rights are concerned, I have no dodbt that these corporations that enter into contracts across the border, and the companies on the other side, all look into the conditions under which the exporting concern is permitted to send out power. I am not so much impressed with the argument that vested rights may be established and that we shall not be able to get away from them when we like. I repeat however that the water is flowing under the bridge continuously and if we do not use it to-day the same water will not flow 'by to-morrow or the next day. If the figures given by my hon. friend (Mr. McMaster) are correct, we have 14,000,000 horse-power in the province of Quebec alone of which he says 1,000,000 horse-power is developed. Although I have not been here continuously, I want to bring a few facts to the attention of the government before any action is taken which will occasion irreparable damage, certainly to Ontario and I think to Quebec as well. We hear a good deal about a surplus of power. Well, there is a surplus of ice on the hottest day if you get to the Arctic; but there is no1 surplus of power where it is wanted. There is no surplus of power to-day which is convenient. I wonder what the government are thinking of when they listen to this talk about a surplus of power, when they know that Toronto has to put up $10,000,000 as a result of delays in connection with the St. Lawrence. They know that the whole of the power at Niagara Falls has been exhausted and that, after waiting for years and years to get some action in connection with the St. Lawrence, the Hydro commission, in the protection of the people of all the municipalities concerned, have been obliged in Toronto to put in a steam auxiliary at a cost of $10,000,000 to the people. power exported from the Ontario company's plant into the United States.

My right hon. friend laughs; it is the only thing he can do, because he has no defence whatever. The power with respect to orders in council is not ordinarily exercised when the House is in session; there is then no excuse for action of that kind. I agreed with the leader of the opposition that the St. Lawrence waterway development should not be discussed without our giving him fair notice. Now, I want to get back to this Carillon power. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre is one of the gentlemen who gave this lease for the development of the Carillon power. And they granted the lease for the development of the Carillon power a few days before the general election in December, 1921. What has that to do with the export of power?

The export; nobody is against the development.

Now, I want to get this matter where it belongs, because this government has not done as much as the late government. did in regard to the development of the Carillon power.
Except talk.
My right hon. friend does not like this part of it. I am not saying he did wrong; I am saying it was a little shady to rush it through a few days before the election in 1921.

permit me? He is making rather unfair
I am telling the truth, according to the record.
-unfair insinuations-

Mr. STEVENS': I want to point out this to the Prime Minister as the leader of the government, without any disrespect to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, that during the discussion of the estimates of this department we have made excellent progress with very large and very important items. We come to this -item to-night, and I intimated in my previous remarks that this raised perhaps the most important and significant question before parliament; I qualified it in this way, that if it was not the most important it was one of the most important questions. To my mind it is the most important. I made that statement, if the minister will recall, before the little tiff between myself and the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham)-
Let us forget it.

-which apparently has occasioned this impasse. I had no intention of delaying the committee or causing any unreasonable discussion, but I submit to the government and to the Prime Minister that in view of the tremendous significance and importance of the question this item should be allowed to stand. I am not asking the government to give way on anything; simply on the meritsl of the case I ask that this item be allowed1 to stand until we have had the documents and other information which we have asked for.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Would it satisfy the committee to let the first litem, salaries of staff, the second item, travelling expenses, and the fourth item, International Electrotechnical Commission, pass, and allow the third item, export of electrical ipower $500, to stand?
The point is that it is all one item.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If consent is given the one item can stand and the other three pass.

The Prime Minister at 12.30 agreed that this item should stand provided we would agree to take up some new items and let them go through. It was a strange suggestion to make at 12.30 after we had got through to-day two resolutions of the Minister of Finance, both very important; the second reading of the budget resolutions as a bill and the debate on an amendment; and some further bills to-night, and then made some progress on the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. That is the treatment this government has had from the opposition. They have never had anything in the nature of obstruction for an hour of the whole of this parliament. There has
been ample progress made to-day, and now we are not allowed to have an item stand except conditionally-an item that involves as big a question as ever was before the people of Canada, an item on which that question can alone be appropriately discussed. Before we can get that to stand pending the bringing down of what is admitted to be important information, we must submit to conditions. That is supposed to be reasonable treatment, and this is propounded to us at one o'clock in the morning. We are not anxious to hold up the item, but we are anxious that there should be reasonable discussion in the light of reasonable information on this item. I am prepared to allow the item to pass if I get the undertaking from the minister that on the next item that comes up in his department, when he presents his estimates again, we can have the discussion finished, he having brought down the information asked for. The understanding is that we can then have a full discussion on this same subject.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Certainly.

I had an arrangement similar to this two years ago, but I was told afterwards that it was illegal. I do not desire that we should be caught that way again. The arrangement should be clearly understood so that there will be no question about the right to go on with this discussion on whatever item is now fixed.
The next item taken up, I said, and the material brought down.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The right hon. leader of the opposition has made a suggestion which I think will meet the situation, and I am prepared on behalf of the government to accept it in the spirit in which it is made.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The understanding is that on the next item introduced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce the debate will continue on the question of the export of electrical power-the same as this item that has been debated under this vote in committee; and that is accepted, I understand, by the right hon. leader of the opposition.

Item agreed to.
